micro.idea: How people decide what to buy. Raise a price and fewer buy; how many fewer depends on how much they want it.
micro.formula: elasticity = % change in sales ÷ % change in price
micro.example: Coffee $4.00 → $4.40 (+10%), sales 200 → 170 (−15%). Revenue falls from $800 to $748.
micro.tip: Change prices in small steps and watch revenue.

macro.idea: The whole economy: growth, recessions, inflation, interest rates. You can't control it, but it moves your sales and costs.
macro.example: Sales up 6% while prices everywhere rose 4%: you really sold about 2% more.
macro.tip: In a slowdown, protect cash. Don't panic-cut prices.

game.idea: When your result depends on a rival's move too. If you both keep cutting prices, you both lose.
game.formula: best move = best result, given what they'll do back
game.example: You cut 20%, the rival matches. Same customers as before, less money for both.
game.tip: Compete on what they can't copy fast: quality and service.

finacct.idea: Three standard reports: profit (income statement), what you own and owe (balance sheet), and where cash went (cash flow).
finacct.example: $12k cash + $8k equipment = $20k owned. Owe the bank $5k → $15k is the owners'.
finacct.tip: Profit up but cash down? Check the cash flow tab.

mgmtacct.idea: Numbers for decisions inside the business: what things really cost, and which costs grow with sales.
mgmtacct.example: Sales $20k, ingredients $8k = 40%. The usual is 25–35%, so look for waste.
mgmtacct.tip: A cost growing faster than sales is the first thing to fix.

markets.idea: Where money is lent and invested: banks, bonds and stock markets. Their rates set what money costs you.
markets.example: $25,000 at 10% costs about $2,500 a year, around $208 a month.
markets.tip: Borrow when the money earns more than its interest.

corpfin.idea: How a business pays for itself and its growth: its own profits, loans, or selling a share.
corpfin.example: $50,000 at 10% over 3 years ≈ $1,613 a month. Only the interest part is a cost.
corpfin.tip: Make sure repayments fit inside your monthly profit.

valuation.idea: What a business is worth. Small firms often sell for a few times their yearly profit.
valuation.formula: value ≈ multiple × yearly profit + cash − debt
valuation.tip: Steady profit raises your value more than one big month.

fund.idea: Selling part of your company for cash. The terms decide the price and who gets paid first.
fund.example: $50,000 in at a $150,000 value → they own 25%.
fund.tip: Watch for 2× terms: they get twice their money back first.

excel.idea: Model the business in numbers, then change one to see what happens to profit.
excel.tip: Do the rough sum before you run the month.

unitecon.idea: The profit on one sale, and how many sales it takes to cover your fixed costs.
unitecon.formula: break-even = fixed costs ÷ (price − cost per sale)
unitecon.example: $9,000 rent and wages ÷ $3 profit a coffee = 3,000 a month, about 100 a day.
unitecon.tip: Can't serve that many? Change price, costs or staff first.

budget.idea: Planning money ahead. Runway is how many months your cash lasts at the current loss.
budget.example: $18,000 cash, losing $4,500 a month → 4 months to turn it around.
budget.tip: Keep at least 3 months of runway.

fsa.idea: Reading the statements to judge health: is it profitable, does profit turn into cash, can it pay its bills?
fsa.formula: cash change = profit − more owed to you − more stock + more you owe
fsa.example: Profit $6,000, but clients owe $9,000 more: cash falls $3,000.

marketing.idea: Getting the right customers to find you, want you and come back.
marketing.formula: return on ads = sales from ads ÷ ad cost
marketing.example: $1,000 of ads → $3,500 sales. At a 40% margin that's $1,400 profit: worth it.
marketing.tip: Spend more only while it pays back.

pricing.idea: Setting prices on what customers value, not just on your costs.
pricing.example: 40 hours at $50 = $2,000. Worth $5,000 to the client? A $3,500 fixed price earns more.
pricing.tip: Always full? Your price is probably too low.

sales.idea: Selling it yourself early on: finding first customers, listening, closing deals.
sales.formula: sales = leads × win rate × average deal
sales.tip: Talk to customers in town. They tell you what to fix.

strategy.idea: Choosing where to compete and how to win: what you will and won't do.
strategy.example: One café is cheapest, the other has the best coffee and seats to work. Both can win.
strategy.tip: Scout your rival, then serve who they serve badly.

ops.idea: Running the daily work: how much you can serve, how fast, at what cost.
ops.example: 2 baristas serve 160 a day. 200 come → 40 leave. 80 come → half the wages wasted.
ops.tip: Match staff and stock to demand.

innov.idea: Finding, testing and launching new ideas while the business keeps running.
innov.example: Developers build a new feature: slower for a while, then customers a rival can't reach.
innov.tip: Try new things in small, affordable steps.

lead.idea: Getting the best from people: hire well, set clear goals, keep workloads fair.
lead.example: $12k wages on $20k sales = 60%. Lose a quarter of the work and it can't pay.
lead.tip: Hire after several busy months, not one.

nego.idea: Reaching a deal when both sides want something. Trade what's cheap for you but valuable to them.
nego.example: Client wants 20% off. Offer 10% off for a longer contract paid upfront.
nego.tip: On news cards, give up time or terms before cash.

law.idea: Contracts make deals enforceable: who does what, by when, and what if they don't.
law.example: A client won't pay for extra changes. Your contract charges them by the hour, so the bill stands.
law.tip: Cheap choices now can bring a bill later.

discovery.idea: Finding out what customers really need before you build or sell much.
discovery.example: Office workers say they've no time to queue. Fast ordering beats a cheaper sandwich.
discovery.tip: Ask customers in town. It's real information.

bizmodel.idea: How a business makes money: who pays, for what, and how often.
bizmodel.example: A café earns a little from many people daily. Software earns a monthly fee for years.
bizmodel.tip: Play all four businesses to see the difference.

launch.idea: Getting from idea to paying customers with little money. Start small, test, grow what works.
launch.formula: months to survive = starting cash ÷ monthly loss
launch.example: $20,000 to start, losing $3,000 a month → about 6 months to break even.
launch.tip: If it can't work on paper, it won't work in the game.

product.idea: Building what customers use and value. A disappointing product loses people, whatever the marketing.
product.example: Customers leave over one missing feature. Building it beats winning sign-ups who'd also leave.
product.tip: Many cancelling? Fix the product before more ads.

saas.idea: Subscription numbers: monthly revenue (MRR), cancellations (churn), and what a customer is worth vs what they cost to win.
saas.formula: LTV = monthly profit ÷ churn; aim for LTV ≥ 3 × CAC
saas.example: $25 profit a month ÷ 5% churn = $500 LTV. Winning one costs $150: healthy.
saas.tip: Lower churn raises LTV the most.

growth.idea: Winning customers efficiently: find what works, measure the cost, spend where it pays.
growth.example: $4,000 of ads → 50 customers = $80 each. $60 profit a month pays it back within 2 months.
growth.tip: Raise marketing in steps and watch the cost per customer.
